issues.legal_issue: A party cannot impeach a witness’s testimony on a material point by alleging its falsity without first giving the witness an opportunity to address that allegation in cross-examination.
material_facts: The tenant challenged the finding that the demand notice had been refused, arguing that the postman was not on duty on the dates recorded and that the refusal endorsement was incorrect.
The postman testified that the tenant refused the notice, but the tenant did not suggest to him in cross-examination that he was not on duty or that the endorsement was incorrect.
The finding of refusal and the resulting eviction order had been upheld by the appellate tribunal and the High Court.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the challenge to service of the notice and dismissed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 138 and 146 of the Evidence Act, 1872, provide for cross-examination and permit questions to test a witness’s veracity. A party intending to suggest that a witness is untruthful on a particular point must put that allegation to the witness in cross-examination and afford an opportunity to explain it; otherwise, the party cannot later impeach the witness on that basis. The Court relied on State of U.P. v. Nahar Singh (dead) and others, which quoted and applied the principle stated in Browne v. Dunn.

predicates.rent_eviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal arising from an eviction order in a rent case.
predicates.witness_testified_to_refusal: A witness testified that the recipient refused the notice.
predicates.challenge_not_put_in_cross_examination: The party disputing the witness’s account did not put the specific allegation of inaccuracy to the witness in cross-examination.

issues.definition: When a rent eviction appeal challenges a witness’s testimony that a notice was refused, but the alleged inaccuracy was not put to the witness in cross-examination, the challenge to service is rejected.
